audience: Engineers with basic programming knowledge learning cap. Explain concepts directly and connect their mechanisms, consequences and design choices. Examples are optional when they clarify a concept; assessment does not require a recurring application, brand names or an example on every card.
prerequisites: A program runs instructions, holds data in memory and can call other code; separate processes do not automatically share their memory.
A network can carry messages between computers, and messages can be delayed or fail to arrive.
An HTTP request has a method, URL, headers and optional body; its response has a status, headers and optional body.
A client requests work from a server; a database stores data that an application can read and change.

objectives.description: Define CAP as a limit on simultaneous consistency and availability guarantees when a distributed data system is partitioned.
Explain a partition as communication failure between running nodes and partition tolerance as defined behavior despite it.
Explain CAP consistency as a single-copy, real-time operation order rather than eventual convergence or database validity rules.
Define CAP availability by operation completion at each non-failing node and distinguish it from uptime percentages, immediate replies and error replies.
Derive the conflict from an isolated reader unable to learn a completed remote write.
Explain how stopping affected operations preserves a single-copy view and what users experience.
Explain serving partitioned requests despite stale or divergent state and the resulting reconciliation obligation.
Define eventual consistency conditionally and distinguish convergence from immediate visibility or preservation of all user intent.
Use required operation semantics and partition behavior to justify a design without universal CP/AP product labels.

questions.question: What system situation does CAP describe? Define distributed data copies at a basic level and state the conditional limit CAP places on consistency and availability. Why is choosing any two letters at all times misleading? Define a network partition and distinguish it from every node crashing. Can both sides remain alive and reachable by clients? Explain what partition tolerance means and why deciding not to discuss partitions does not prevent them in a distributed deployment.
criteria: Distributed data copies reside on different networked nodes and must communicate to coordinate changes.
When a partition prevents required communication, a system cannot guarantee both one-copy consistency and completion of every request at non-failing nodes for the affected data.
The conflict is conditional on partitioned communication, not a general menu of any two features or a claim that healthy systems cannot provide both.
A partition prevents communication between some nodes; the nodes can remain running and independently reachable by clients.
Partition tolerance concerns system behavior despite that communication failure; it does not mean every operation must remain available and consistent.
A deployment using networked nodes can encounter lost or delayed communication; omitting the failure from a design does not remove it.
criticalMisconceptions: CAP always requires choosing any two letters.

questions.question: Explain CAP consistency using a completed write followed by a later read of the same data, with no intervening write. What must the read observe? How are overlapping operations treated, and how does this differ from eventual convergence or preserving valid database records? What does CAP availability require of requests reaching a non-failing node? Must completion be instantaneous or within a specified latency target? Explain why refusing an affected operation or merely returning an error is not a successful way to preserve both CAP properties, and why an uptime percentage is a different measure.
criteria: CAP consistency is linearizability: operations appear to take effect in one order that respects completed-before-started relationships.
With no intervening write, a read starting after a write completes observes that write; overlapping operations may be ordered either way if the resulting single-copy order remains valid.
Eventual convergence allows temporary old reads, and database validity constraints are a different meaning of consistency.
Every request to a non-failing node must eventually complete with the response required by the operation; the theorem does not set a practical response-time bound.
Indefinite waiting or refusal to perform the affected operation sacrifices this availability; a generic error reply does not turn refusal into a successful read or write.
Operational uptime or latency targets measure practical service quality and do not replace the theorem's per-request definition.
criticalMisconceptions: CAP consistency is merely all copies agreeing eventually.
Any HTTP reply, including refusing the operation, proves CAP availability.

questions.question: Two replicas initially hold value 0 and cannot communicate. A client completes a write of 1 at replica A; later another client reads from still-running replica B with no other writes. Explain what B knows, what consistency requires, and why returning 0, refusing/waiting indefinitely, or guessing 1 cannot guarantee both properties across possible writes.
criteria: B knows its prior value but cannot learn A's completed write through the partition; consistency requires the later read to reflect 1.
Returning the known old value violates consistency; refusing or waiting indefinitely sacrifices availability for that read.
Guessing cannot guarantee correctness across possible unseen values; the information barrier, not a particular product weakness, causes the conflict.

questions.question: How can a system preserve CAP consistency during a partition? Explain why only operations that can safely preserve the required order may continue, what happens to unsafe reads or writes, and whether this necessarily shuts down every operation on every node. How can a system preserve availability for requests on separated live nodes, and which consistency guarantee does it give up? Distinguish stale reads from conflicting accepted writes and explain what reconciliation must address after communication returns. Does continuing requests ensure no updates are lost or preserve every cross-record business rule?
criteria: The system restricts operations to those that can establish the required single-copy order and refuses or waits on unsafe operations.
Affected clients experience failed or delayed operations, which gives up availability for those operations.
Unaffected or safely coordinated operations may continue; favoring consistency need not mean shutting down the entire system.
Nodes continue using locally available state, so a read may miss a completed remote write and violate linearizability.
If separated nodes accept incompatible writes, copies may diverge and require an explicit merge or conflict-resolution policy when they communicate again.
Availability alone supplies neither a safe merge nor protection against lost intent or broken cross-record rules; those depend on application and storage policy.

questions.question: Define eventual consistency and state the conditions under which copies are expected to converge. Does it specify a fixed catch-up deadline, guarantee read-your-writes, or ensure every concurrent update's intent survives? Explain why reconciliation policy still matters. Compare an operation that must never return a value older than a completed write with one allowed to return a temporarily old value while reachable nodes keep answering. State the behavior each should allow during a split and after recovery, including client-visible failure or staleness and any conflict policy. Explain why the decision concerns operation guarantees and configuration rather than permanently labeling an entire vendor, and whether CAP alone decides normal-operation latency and cost.
criteria: If new updates stop and communication and propagation resume under the system's reconciliation rules, copies eventually converge.
Eventual consistency alone gives no fixed deadline or immediate read-your-writes guarantee.
Convergence means agreement on a resulting state, not preservation of every conflicting intent; resolution policies determine the outcome.
The strict operation must reject or delay where the guarantee cannot be established; the stale-tolerant operation can continue from local state while accepting weaker consistency.
The design states user-visible unavailability or staleness, and how propagation or conflicting writes are handled after communication returns.
Choices depend on operation and configuration; CAP does not by itself determine healthy-operation latency, capacity or operational cost.
criticalMisconceptions: Eventual consistency automatically means no concurrent update can be lost.
